content_voiceover: This slide is the same treatment landscape you just saw, but now filtered through Taiwan's National Health Insurance reimbursement rules, which is exactly the kind of local, practical detail that shows up on board exams here. Notice the light gray shading appearing in the salvage unfit column, gemtuzumab ozogamicin, venetoclax plus HMA, and gilteritinib are all marked as not reimbursed by NHI in that particular indication, even though they are clinically used and available. Venetoclax combined with FLAG-Ida in the fit salvage setting is shown grayed out too, meaning it's not reimbursed there either. Meanwhile agents like enasidenib and revumenib remain simply not available in Taiwan at all, shown in dark gray, a distinct category from not reimbursed. This distinction matters clinically, a drug can be approved and physically available but still require self-payment or a special application, which changes real-world treatment decisions even when the evidence supports using it.
keypoints: Same treatment map, now annotated with Taiwan NHI reimbursement status
Light gray equals available but not reimbursed by NHI
Dark gray equals not available in Taiwan at all
Salvage unfit agents like gilteritinib and venetoclax plus HMA are not reimbursed
Reimbursement status can limit real-world use despite drug availability
keypoint_voiceover: Two shades of gray carry different meanings here, light gray means the drug is available in Taiwan but the National Health Insurance won't pay for it in that setting, dark gray means the drug isn't available in Taiwan at all. Recognizing that distinction is a good local-context board question.
